extracted.intended_audience: students (undergraduate/introductory) learning to write mathematical proofs; mathematics instructors and TAs preparing solution writeups
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and conventions for composing clear, readable, and conventional mathematical proofs (statement, structure, notation, exposition, and formatting). Intended to teach students and instructors how to present proofs appropriately for textbooks, solution manuals, or coursework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know your audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Have a clear idea of the intended audience so you can give the right amount of information at the proper level of sophistication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust level of detail depending on audience (e.g., brief instructor solutions vs. more detailed student solutions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Write a first draft of your proof and then revise it
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't be satisfied with the first draft; write, read over, and refine your proof to ensure readers can understand the reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be clear and concise, include necessary details but avoid rambling; practice and revision are essential to improve proof-writing skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use complete sentences and proper paragraph structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Conform to accepted rules of grammar; write proofs using complete sentences and avoid run-on sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pay attention to punctuation and sentence structure; use a spell checker when using a word processor; organize exposition into paragraphs each with a simple point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep it simple
rubrics_metrics.description: Use simple, declarative sentences and short paragraphs so that writing does not make the mathematical argument harder to understand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each paragraph should have a single simple point; avoid unnecessarily complex or convoluted wording.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin with a carefully worded statement of the theorem or result to be proven
rubrics_metrics.description: State the theorem as a simple declarative statement (do not merely rewrite the exercise phrasing like 'Show that' or 'Prove that').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Then skip a line, write 'Proof' (italics or boldface when using a word processor) and begin the proof on the same line; ensure paragraphs are easily identified (blank line or indentation). Example: 'Theorem. If x and y are odd integers, then x+y is an odd integer. Proof: We assume that x and y are odd integers . . . .'

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin the proof with a statement of your assumptions and what you will prove
rubrics_metrics.description: Immediately follow the theorem statement with a clear listing of assumptions and a precise statement of the goal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Proof. We assume that x and y are odd integers and will prove that x+y is an odd integer.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the pronoun 'we'
rubrics_metrics.description: Write in the first-person plural when using pronouns in proofs to emphasize collaboration between writer and reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using 'we' encourages the reader to work through the mathematics together and is the standard convention (e.g., 'We assume that ...').

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep the reader informed about proof method and status of assertions
rubrics_metrics.description: Tell the reader early if you will use a particular method (contrapositive, contradiction, induction) and indicate whether assertions are assumptions, previously proven results, or well-known facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide explicit signal phrases like 'We will prove this result by proving the contrapositive', 'We will prove this statement using a proof by contradiction', 'We will use mathematical induction to prove this result.' Also explicitly state when a step follows from a hypothesis or a cited theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use italics for variables and appropriate font conventions when using a word processor
rubrics_metrics.description: Typeset mathematics to resemble typeset mathematics: italicize variables, use boldface for vectors, and use upright/regular font for mathematical function names (e.g., trig and log functions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not write 'sin(x)' with letters spaced oddly; instead typeset as sin(x) with proper font styles. Ensure your word processor can produce appropriate mathematical symbols and formatting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use $ for multiplication or ^ for exponents (avoid programming notation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid coding-style notation like '*' or '^' or inline ASCII fractions in formal mathematical writing because it is hard for humans to read.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write fractions and powers in conventional mathematical form; for complex fractions, use stacked fractions rather than linear '=/'. Example of hard-to-read: '!x3 % 3x2 + 1/2' is worse than properly typeset multiline fraction display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Display important equations and mathematical expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Center and display important equations and manipulations with blank lines before and after; do not use two-column 'steps with reasons' formats common in some geometry texts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the left side of an equation does not change, do not repeat it; show algebraic manipulations clearly and let displayed equations form part of the exposition. Example display: 'Using algebra, we obtain x+y = (2m+1)(2n+1) = 4mn + 2m + 2n + 1 = 2(2mn+m+n)+1. Since m and n are integers, we conclude ...'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use equation numbers when you will refer to an equation later
rubrics_metrics.description: Number centered/displayed equations you will refer to later, placing the number in parentheses at the right margin on the same line as the equation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Number only those equations you will reference. When referring to an equation by number, the usual convention is to write 'equation (1)' (lowercase 'equation' is customary). Provide an example: display equation, label (1), then later 'using the result in equation (1), we obtain ...'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use a mathematical symbol at the beginning of a sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid starting sentences with symbols as this hampers readability; instead name the quantity first in English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: 'Let n be an integer. n is an odd integer provided that ...' Better: 'An integer n is odd provided that ...' Recast sentences to begin with words rather than symbols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use English and minimize the use of cumbersome symbolic quantifier notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer English words for quantifiers and connectives in formal mathematical writing instead of symbols like ∀, ∃, |, ∴.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write 'For each real number x, there exists a real number y such that x+y=0' or simply 'Every real number has an additive inverse' rather than writing symbolic quantifier expressions that are harder to read in prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use quantifiers with appropriate words (be explicit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Make quantification explicit using words: use 'for some', 'there exists', 'for each', etc., instead of ambiguous phrasing like 'where' or 'for an integer m'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid 'where' as it often hides quantifier meaning. Replace 'For an integer m, m^2+m is even' with 'For each integer m, m^2+m is even' (for universal) or 'There exists an integer m such that ...' (for existential). Be careful with 'a/an' which can be ambiguous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain how previous results can be used
rubrics_metrics.description: When invoking a theorem, state the theorem and explain how its hypotheses are satisfied before applying its conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'According to Theorem 20, every nonconstant linear function is a bijection. Consequently, because both f and g are nonconstant linear functions, they are injective and surjective. Then, by Theorem 21 (composition of injective functions is injective), since f and g are both injective, f∘g is injective.' Explicitly connect hypotheses to the current situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tell the reader when the proof has been completed
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly signal the end of a proof with a phrase or symbol to make clear that the argument has concluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write 'This completes the proof.' or finish with a sentence that states precisely what has been proven. Use an end-of-proof symbol (e.g., a box, QED, or the suggested '!') as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revise Your First Draft (final reminder)
rubrics_metrics.description: Thoroughly review, edit, and revise your proof; a well-written proof is seldom obtained on the first try.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reiterate earlier advice: do not be satisfied with the first version; editing and refinement are standard practice in writing mathematics well.
